misconceptions.description: Treating a click on 'I Agree' as informed consent
misconceptions.trigger: learner cites clickthrough rate as evidence of consent
misconceptions.feedback: Informed consent requires disclosure, comprehension, voluntariness, and competence. A click satisfies disclosure on a technicality and almost nothing else.

misconceptions.description: Treating consent-flow UI as neutral terrain that does not shape choice
misconceptions.trigger: learner argues that 'Accept All' being big and 'Reject All' being buried is just visual hierarchy
misconceptions.feedback: Asymmetric prominence is a documented dark pattern that defeats voluntariness. Symmetric controls are required by DSA and GDPR enforcement.

misconceptions.description: Believing well-collected individual consent settles the ethics of any deployment
misconceptions.trigger: learner cites unanimous user consent as proof of ethical deployment
misconceptions.feedback: Public goods, deeply asymmetric power, and vulnerable users all need supplementary protections (democratic deliberation, due process, surrogate consent). Consent is one layer.

misconceptions.description: Treating consent as a one-time event that does not require ongoing revocability
misconceptions.trigger: learner ignores withdrawal flows or makes deletion deliberately hard
misconceptions.feedback: Voluntariness extends across time. Real, easy withdrawal is required for consent to remain meaningful. CCPA and GDPR codify this.
